problems.description: Public-signature type hints regressed: get_task/get_tasks/update_task lost their `-> dict | None` / `str | None` annotations, and `title: str = None` is a mypy-incompatible default — contradicts the repo convention of type hints on public signatures.
datetime.utcnow() is deprecated in Python 3.12 and returns naive timestamps; carried forward from the seed rather than replaced.
Module-level `app = create_app()` executes init_db() as an import side effect, so importing app in tests creates todos.db in the cwd; standard Flask pattern but slightly impure.
app.run(debug=True) keeps debug mode on the default entry point — acceptable for a dev story app.

strengths: App-factory pattern with injectable database parameter enables isolated per-test SQLite DBs via tmp_path fixtures.
Removed legacy cruft the seed intentionally planted (_legacy_format_date, _notify_admin, fetch_task alias).
Fixed the seed bug where new tasks were created with status 'done' instead of 'pending'.
Added input validation (non-string and blank titles, empty body) returning proper 400s, plus a stricter title check on PUT.
Comprehensive test suite covering happy and error paths (201, 400s, 404s).
Centralized 400/404 error handlers and preserved the existing section-comment structure.
commit_reviews.summary: Strong session-1 refactor that turns the seeded single-file Flask app into a testable app-factory design with DB dependency injection, a bug fix, real input validation, and a proper test suite — a net architectural improvement, only mildly undercut by the dropped public-signature type hints.

problems.description: Hardcoded fallback SECRET_KEY ('dev-secret-key-change-me') signs every JWT when the env var is unset; in any non-dev deployment this is a known-key forgery. Should fail fast (refuse to start) outside a dev environment rather than silently defaulting.

get_user_by_id/get_user_by_username SELECT * returns the full row including password_hash, which is then carried through token_required even though only user["id"] is needed. Select only the required columns.

token_required is defined inside create_app, re-creating the decorator per app instance and closing over app; works for the factory pattern at this scale but couples auth to a single app object and is untestable in isolation.
tasks.owner_id REFERENCES users(id) with no ON DELETE behavior, and SQLite only enforces FKs with PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON (not set here); owner scoping relies on application checks alone.

No tests added for the new auth paths (register/login/token validation) despite +32 functions and +394 lines; auth is security-critical and the register/login/token flows are exactly what should be regression-covered.

strengths: Auth + per-user task ownership is a coherent feature for a task-manager story and is cleanly scoped to a single well-structured diff (+394/-61 in app.py only)
Respects existing patterns: app-factory, module-level model functions with database= kwarg, section-comment headers, existing error handlers and CRUD shapes all preserved
Conventions held in new code: snake_case functions, UPPER_CASE module constants (SECRET_KEY, TOKEN_TTL), consistent comment style — no new violations introduced
Defensive migration via PRAGMA table_info column check upgrades older databases in place instead of breaking existing rows
Input validation and proper HTTP semantics (400/401/409/201), password hashing via werkzeug rather than plaintext storage
Owner scoping is applied consistently across every CRUD operation (get_tasks, get_task, update_task) rather than bolted onto routes
commit_reviews.summary: Cleanly-architected auth + ownership feature that respects the existing factory/model-function conventions (note: the mechanical 0.71 convention score reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files like celery_config.py, db.py, notifications.py — the added code itself is convention-clean), held back only by a hardcoded fallback SECRET_KEY and a full-row SELECT that exposes password_hash in memory.

problems.description: Email column is added only via ALTER TABLE in init_db; the base CREATE TABLE users statement is not updated to include email, so every fresh database runs a redundant ALTER on top of the CREATE.
Adds celery/redis as runtime dependencies (celery_config.py, notifications.py) with no visible requirements.txt update in the commit, leaving the new feature non-reproducible on a clean checkout.

Completion detection fetches the previous task state before update_task on every PUT, adding an unconditional read and relying on read-then-write ordering that could miss notifications under concurrent status updates.

Module-level config constants in celery_config.py use snake_case (broker_url, result_backend) while the codebase convention is UPPER_CASE; Celery accepts lowercase but it conflicts with the measured convention style.
Email is not format-validated and the notification recipient silently falls back to the username when no email is registered, so arbitrary user-controlled strings can be used as the delivery address.

strengths: Clean async boundary: the Celery task lives in a dedicated notifications.py module with explicit queue routing (task_routes) and a namespaced task name matching its module path.
Correct transition detection — the prior task state is fetched before the update, so already-completed, non-completed, and title-only updates do not re-trigger or spuriously trigger notifications.
Strong test coverage of the trigger edge cases (no retrigger on already-completed, no fire on non-completed/title-only updates, registered-email precedence) via mocked .delay() calls.
The email migration mirrors the existing owner_id migration pattern (test_migration_adds_owner_id_to_legacy_tasks_table), and the change reuses the established get_task/get_user_by_id model helpers.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-tested integration that adds async email notifications on task completion with correct transition detection and Celery isolation, at the cost of a slightly redundant in-place migration, an undeclared celery/redis dependency, and minor convention deviations.

problems.description: Measured convention score 0.71 with 19 violations across db.py, notifications.py, celery_config.py, __init__.py (class casing, snake_case functions, UPPER_CASE constants). Note: the visible app.py diff is clean, so the bulk of the violations fall in files outside the shown diff — flagging the discrepancy rather than attributing them all to this commit.

generate_password_hash was moved from the model layer (create_user) into the route handler in app.py, mixing password-hashing concern into the controller and splitting it from where the hash is consumed.
Repository objects are constructed inside create_app and captured in route closures rather than injected or scoped per-request, which is acceptable but may complicate testing and future DI.

strengths: Clean layered refactor: SQL access extracted to db.py, data access to repositories.py (TaskRepository/UserRepository), leaving app.py as pure routing/controller layer — respects the existing pattern and reduces app.py surface drastically.

Repository methods are well-named and behavior-preserving (find_by_id, find_by_username, find_all_by_owner map 1:1 to prior model functions), so the refactor keeps the existing DB schema and migrations intact.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid architectural refactor toward a repository layer that improves separation of concerns and reduces app.py by ~120 lines, dragged down only by a measured convention score of 0.71 whose violations sit mostly outside the visible diff.

problems.description: Rate limiter hard-couples the app to Redis (storage_uri=REDIS_URL); if Redis is unreachable every limited endpoint errors instead of degrading — no in-memory fallback is configured though Flask-Limiter supports one.

A single shared 100/min budget (scope='api') spans all endpoints, so heavy use of one route (e.g. a chatty list_tasks consumer) can exhaust the entire per-key quota, including login/register for the same user.
Tests were updated for the new response envelope, but no new tests cover pagination edge cases (invalid cursor/limit, limit clamping, has_more boundary, next_cursor semantics, the 429 handler).

Mechanical convention score 0.71 flags 19 violations, but the listed ones (db.py, notifications.py, celery_config.py, __init__.py PascalCase/snake_case/UPPER_CASE) are concentrated in pre-existing modules; the new code itself is snake_case, documented, and constant-cased — the measurement overstates this commit's own style debt.

strengths: Rate-limit key design is well-reasoned: per-user budget when authenticated, per-IP fallback, with an inline comment explaining the intent
Cursor pagination is implemented correctly: stable id-DESC ordering (with rationale vs. created_at), limit+1 has_more detection, and documented next_cursor semantics
key_prefix scoped to the database name isolates counter namespaces between instances/tests
Adds a JSON 429 error handler and headers_enabled for rate-limit transparency
Extends existing patterns faithfully — repository layer, app factory, auth decorator ordering — and updates tests to match the new contract
commit_reviews.summary: The cross_cutting session cleanly adds per-user/IP rate limiting and correct cursor pagination following existing repository/factory/decorator patterns, at the cost of a hard Redis dependency and a single shared per-key budget across all endpoints.

compounding_issues: Seed bugs (bad_seed: create_task inserted status 'done' while returning 'pending'; dead stubs `_legacy_format_date`/`_notify_admin`) were corrected in S1, but any later session relying on the buggy return-vs-stored status would have silently diverged — the fix landed early enough that no session did

S2 added the `users`/`owner_id` columns via an ALTER TABLE migration that leaves pre-existing task rows with NULL owner_id, so unowned tasks are invisible to the owner-scoped queries S4/S5 introduced (a latent data-consistency gap for any carried-over DB)
Binary artifacts (`todos.db`, `__pycache__/*.pyc`) are committed and re-created across sessions (S4 deleted todos.db, S5 re-added it) with no .gitignore — repo hygiene degrades as sessions accumulate

S3 and S5 both hard-couple the app to a live Redis on localhost:6379 (Celery broker/backend + Flask-Limiter storage); the S5 rate-limit test suite fails outright if Redis is down, making the greenfield app's correctness depend on an external service
S2's auth retrofit was the shakiest session (confidence 0.69, 2 retries, single-file change) and set the SECRET_KEY default to a hardcoded dev value that later sessions never hardened
key_decisions: App-factory pattern (`create_app(database=..., rate_limit=...)`) established in S1 enabled per-test tmp-DB isolation and let every later session inject dependencies (rate limit, per-database limiter key_prefix) without global state
S1 proactively removed the bad-seed's dead stubs and fixed the status write/return mismatch rather than building on them — early decontamination of the seed

S2 introduced JWT auth (pyjwt HS256, 24h TTL) with a `token_required` decorator and the task-owner model, which became the foundation for S4's owner-scoped repository queries and S5's per-user rate-limit keys
S3 wired async notifications via Celery with a `newly_completed` transition guard (previous_status != completed) to prevent duplicate emails on idempotent PUTs

S4 refactored the data layer into a BaseRepository hierarchy with incremental ALTER TABLE migrations, preserving the 40-test suite through the reshape — disciplined refactor that did not regress behavior
S5 implemented cursor-based pagination (id DESC, stable under insertion, with next_cursor/total contract) and a Flask-Limiter shared budget keyed per authenticated user with IP fallback
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically across the five sessions. Code grew 143→441 lines and tests 15→63 (final test/code ratio 1.32) with every session exiting 0, all_successful true, and test_executed_success true. Session 1 recovered cleanly from the bad seed (status bug fixed, stubs removed), session 2 was the shakiest moment (confidence 0.69, 2 retries, auth retrofitted onto the existing API), and sessions 3–4 consolidated — S4's repository refactor held the test count at 40 while reshaping the whole data-access layer. Session 5 was the most demanding (580s, $2.13, 53 tool calls, lowest confidence 0.77) yet produced the most tests and the strongest architecture, ending with a well-layered app (routes → repositories → db schema + migrations, auth, async notifications, and rate limiting) whose only weaknesses are operational coupling to Redis and committed binary artifacts.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent five-session arc (greenfield → auth → async notifications → repository refactor → cross-cutting rate-limiting/pagination) that fixed the bad-seed bugs early, steadily deepened architecture without regressing tests, and finished with a clean, well-tested layered API.
